c.tagline: Africa's cocoa isle where the equator meets the Atlantic.

taxi.fareNote: Private taxis negotiate a fixed price before departure (roughly $10 for a 10km trip); shared hiace minivans cover the same routes for a fraction of the cost but leave only once full.

emergency.note: Medical facilities are very limited; serious injuries or illnesses typically require evacuation to Portugal or elsewhere. Comprehensive travel insurance with medevac coverage is strongly recommended.

religion.r: Evangelical/Protestant (Adventist, Assembly of God, New Apostolic, etc.)

hood_landmark.Centro (Downtown): Sé Catedral de Nossa Senhora da Graça, São Tomé

avoid.reason: Petty theft happens on beaches and around the central market, so avoid flashing valuables and skip poorly lit streets after dark.

hood_desc: The historic downtown core around Ana Chaves Bay, with the cathedral, fortress-museum and central market within walking distance; suits first-time visitors who want to explore on foot and stay close to restaurants and shops.

A quiet beachfront strip right beside the airport runway, home to the city's most polished resort-style hotels; ideal for travelers who want easy transfers, a pool, and sea views without needing a taxi.
A laid-back fishing village on the eastern edge of the city with a long black-sand beach and a slower pace; good for those wanting a local, coastal feel away from downtown bustle.
A dense, authentic residential neighborhood just south of the center, popular with volunteers, NGO workers and budget travelers wanting an affordable base close to everything.

The upscale southern seafront avenue near the Presidential Palace, home to São Tomé's top hotels and ocean-view dining; suited to travelers wanting comfort within a short walk or taxi ride of downtown.

water.note: Outdated infrastructure makes tap water unsafe; stick to bottled or treated water.

transit.pay: Fares for hiaces and city buses are paid in cash (dobra) directly to the driver or a conductor when boarding or alighting; there is no smart-card or app-based payment system. Fares are fixed per route rather than metered, so having small notes helps.
transit.hours: Hiaces and buses generally operate from around 6am to 7-8pm; there is little to no public transport after dark, so taxis or pre-arranged drivers are the main after-hours option.
transit.note: Transport is informal and route-based rather than scheduled; vehicles depart from markets and central stops once full. Most visitors combine hiaces for short hops with taxis or rental cars for flexibility.

tip.r: Tipping is not deeply rooted in local custom but is increasingly appreciated at tourist-oriented hotels and restaurants; rounding up or leaving 5-10% is a welcome gesture, not an obligation.

food.name: Calulu de peixe
food.desc: The national dish: smoked or dried fish layered with okra, aubergine, sweet-potato leaves and palm oil, stewed slowly and eaten with angu maize porridge.

places.name: Petisqueira Leo
places.note: Tia Leo's calulu is the version locals and visitors both name first.

places.name: Restaurante Tradicao
places.note: Traditional kitchen best known precisely for its calulu de peixe.

places.name: Restaurante Bar Zima
places.note: Affordable Sao Tomean plates; calulu and fried banana are the ones to order.

food.name: Banana com peixe
food.desc: Fish grilled over coals or cooked in palm oil, served with slices of fried plantain, rice and greens - the island's everyday lunch, and hard to better.

places.name: Carambola
places.note: Serves peixe azeite grilled with fried banana, rice and vegetables.

places.name: Tia Zada
places.note: Beachside kitchen doing very fresh fish and octopus with banana and breadfruit at low prices.

places.name: Restaurante Bar Zima
places.note: Grilled fish and fried bananas are the standout orders here.

food.name: Polvo guisado
food.desc: Octopus stewed until tender in palm oil, onion, tomato and chilli, or grilled and dressed with lime; the sea is minutes from every table in the capital.

places.name: Petisqueira Leo
places.note: Stewed octopus and grilled fish are what regulars come for besides the calulu.

places.name: Tia Zada
places.note: Octopus served with fried banana and breadfruit for a few dollars.

places.name: Carambola
places.note: Traditional Sao Tomean seafood cooking in a relaxed setting.

food.name: Feijoada santomense
food.desc: Beans slow-cooked with smoked fish or pork, palm oil and island greens - the Portuguese dish rebuilt around what grows on the equator.

places.name: Restaurante Tradicao
places.note: Sticks to the old island recipes; bean stews and calulu are the backbone of the menu.

places.name: Petisqueira Leo
places.note: Home-style cooking with a rotating list of Sao Tomean stews.

places.name: Mercado Municipal food stalls
places.note: Market cook shops serve stews and rice to traders from mid-morning at local prices.

food.name: Fruta-pao and matabala
food.desc: Breadfruit and taro boiled or fried as the island's staple starches, served beside fish; along with jackfruit and safu they define the Sao Tomean plate.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: See them raw and enormous, then buy them cooked from the stalls behind.

places.name: Tia Zada
places.note: Serves breadfruit and banana as the standard sides with seafood.

places.name: Restaurante Tradicao
places.note: Uses the island roots as sides rather than importing potatoes.

food.name: Sao Tome chocolate and cocoa
food.desc: The island was once the world's largest cocoa producer; single-estate bars, cocoa nibs and cocoa-pulp sweets are now its most famous export.

places.name: Claudio Corallo chocolate house
places.note: Tastings of single-estate bars and cocoa spirits from the plantations on Principe and Sao Tome.

places.name: Roca Agostinho Neto
places.note: Historic plantation estate where cocoa is still grown and sold to visitors.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Raw cocoa, cocoa paste and island coffee sold loose alongside spices and vanilla.

food.name: Vinho de palma
food.desc: Sap tapped from palm trunks at dawn and drunk the same day - milky, faintly sour, lightly alcoholic; by evening it has fermented into something stronger.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Tappers sell it by the bottle in the early morning, at its freshest and mildest.

places.name: Praia Gamboa beach bars
places.note: Informal shacks pour palm wine alongside beer through the afternoon.

places.name: Roadside stalls toward Trindade
places.note: Villages along the road sell palm wine straight from the tapping gourds.

food.name: Cacharamba
food.desc: Rough sugarcane spirit distilled on the island, often re-steeped with honey, ginger or cocoa into a ponche; ordered in small glasses, not large ones.

places.name: Restaurante Bar Zima
places.note: Bar as much as restaurant; good place to try the local spirit and infusions.

places.name: Claudio Corallo chocolate house
places.note: Sells refined cocoa-infused spirits and liqueurs made on the estate.

places.name: Mercado Municipal
places.note: Bottled cacharamba and honey-ginger ponche sold by market vendors.

landmarks: Fort São Sebastião
This 16th-century Portuguese fortress guarding the harbor now houses the National Museum, its weathered ramparts and lighthouse offering a vivid link to colonial history.
Sé Cathedral (Nossa Senhora da Graça)
One of Africa's oldest cathedrals, this whitewashed 16th-century church with its red-trimmed tower anchors the historic center and remains the city's spiritual landmark.
Presidential Palace
The elegant colonial-era Palácio Presidencial, with its pastel facade and manicured gardens, serves as the seat of government and a striking architectural centerpiece.
Boca do Inferno
A dramatic natural blowhole where Atlantic waves crash through volcanic rock and erupt skyward, making it one of the island's most photographed natural spectacles.
Ilhéu das Rolas
A tiny island straddling the Equator just off São Tomé's southern tip, famous for its monument marking 0° latitude and pristine beaches.
Praia Jalé
A wild, palm-fringed black-and-gold sand beach on the island's remote coast, cherished by travelers seeking dramatic, unspoiled scenery away from the crowds.
Pico Cão Grande
A surreal 663-meter volcanic spire piercing the rainforest canopy, this needle-shaped peak is the island's most iconic and photographed natural landmark.
Roça São João dos Angolares
A beautifully restored former cocoa plantation estate whose grand faded architecture tells the story of São Tomé's colonial cocoa boom and its complex legacy.
Óbô Natural Park
A vast rainforest reserve covering much of the island's interior, teeming with endemic birds and dramatic volcanic peaks, drawing hikers and nature lovers alike.
National Assembly Building
The seat of São Tomé and Príncipe's legislature, this distinctive colonial-style building in the capital reflects the nation's small but proud democratic institutions.

train.note: São Tomé & Príncipe has no railway of any kind. Getting around the island is by shared minibuses (taxis colectivos) from the market in São Tomé town, private taxi or rental car.

bus.note: It is an island nation, so there are no international road/coach routes. Local transport is informal shared minibuses linking São Tomé town with towns like Trindade, Neves and Santana; there is no formal operator or online booking.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries. Travel between the two islands (São Tomé and Príncipe) is normally by air; the sea link is served only by occasional/irregular cargo boats, so most visitors fly with STP Airways. Confirm any boat locally before relying on it.

full.name: Port-Gentil
full.blurb: Gabonese port city on the Atlantic coast known for its oil industry and lagoons.
